foundation.title: Before the cases: how a quantum algorithm gets access to data and matrices
foundation.lead: A quantum algorithm is not given a NumPy array for free. Before discussing speedups, we must say how classical data, matrix entries, or a linear operator become quantum operations. State preparation, query oracles, and block encodings are three different access contracts.

accessModels.name: State preparation
accessModels.plain: Build a circuit P that creates the input quantum state you actually want to use.
accessModels.why: Algorithms that start from amplitude-encoded data need this state before any later quantum subroutine can help. Preparation cost is therefore part of the end-to-end algorithm, not decorative preprocessing.
accessModels.example: The Pauli-X and Hadamard cases show the smallest exact examples.

accessModels.name: Digital query oracle
accessModels.plain: Ask a reversible black box for a matrix entry encoded in a work register.
accessModels.why: Query-complexity theorems often count how many times the oracle is called, but a real fault-tolerant implementation must also build the arithmetic and memory circuit hidden inside that call.
accessModels.example: The GHL Robin paper explicitly contrasts this model with its gate-level construction.

accessModels.name: Block encoding
accessModels.plain: Embed a possibly non-unitary matrix A as the clean ancilla block of a larger unitary U_A.
accessModels.why: Quantum hardware applies unitary gates. Block encoding is the interface that lets algorithms such as QSVT and Hamiltonian simulation manipulate a general structured matrix through a unitary circuit.
accessModels.example: BE Case 1, the cubic diagonal family, and the Robin case all certify this contract.

circuitLegend: A horizontal wire is one qubit/register. Time flows from left to right.
A ket at the left fixes the input state of that wire.
A box is a gate. Its matrix acts when the state reaches that box.
A control dot means another gate acts only when the control condition is satisfied.
U† means the inverse/conjugate-transpose circuit; it often uncomputes temporary information.
An ancilla is workspace. A clean block-encoding proof normally requires selected ancillas to start and end in |0>.
Measurement converts quantum amplitudes into classical outcomes; it is different from the coherent unitary part of the circuit.

pauli-x-state-preparation.readerGoal: Learn what state preparation means before seeing a complicated data-loading circuit.
pauli-x-state-preparation.whyThisCase: A quantum algorithm must begin in a quantum state. This one-qubit example isolates that input-access problem: can a circuit take the easy state |0> to the requested target |1>?
pauli-x-state-preparation.algorithmContext: This is not claiming a speedup. It is the smallest possible instance of the same contract used when a larger algorithm asks for an input state |psi>.
circuitReading: The X box swaps the amplitudes of |0> and |1>.
The output is exactly |1>; there is no ancilla and no measurement in the certificate.

theorems.label: Case theorem
theorems.title: Pauli X prepares the basis state |1>
theorems.statementProse: The target vector is normalized, X is unitary, and applying X to the zero basis state returns the target exactly.
proofSteps: Normalize the target
The target has one amplitude equal to 1 and all others 0, so its norm is 1.
Prove unitarity
X is a permutation matrix and therefore preserves the computational basis and inner products.
Check the zero input
The first column of X is exactly the vector |1>.
Package the certificate
The target, circuit, semantic proof, and one-gate resource record are stored together.

hadamard-plus-state-preparation.readerGoal: See the difference between a classical random bit and a coherent quantum superposition.
hadamard-plus-state-preparation.whyThisCase: Many quantum algorithms need interference. The Hadamard gate is the smallest example where two basis states simultaneously have nonzero amplitudes before measurement.
hadamard-plus-state-preparation.algorithmContext: Preparing |+> is the first step of countless circuits. The important lesson is that amplitudes, not classical probabilities, are transformed coherently by later gates.
circuitReading: The wire is |0>, so the amplitude vector is (1,0).
A computational-basis measurement would return 0 or 1 with equal probability, but before measurement the relative amplitudes can still interfere.

theorems.label: Case theorem
theorems.title: Hadamard prepares the equal superposition
theorems.statementProse: The exact square-root normalization, unitarity of H, and equality of the zero-input column with |+> are all machine checked.
proofSteps: Normalize |+>
Each amplitude has squared magnitude 1/2, so the total is 1.
Prove H is unitary
The two columns are normalized and orthogonal.
Read column zero
Multiplying by |0> selects H's first column, which is the desired amplitude vector.
Record the circuit
The exact preparation uses one H gate and no ancilla.

be-case-1-champion.readerGoal: Understand why a non-unitary map needs a larger unitary before a quantum circuit can implement it.
be-case-1-champion.whyThisCase: The transfer E1 maps one labelled sector of the system into another and is not itself a unitary gate. The case shows the basic block-encoding trick without hiding behind a large oracle: add one clean signal qubit and complete the desired action to a reversible permutation.
be-case-1-champion.algorithmContext: This is the finite toy model for the general situation in scientific computing: the linear map you care about is often not unitary, while the quantum circuit must be.
circuitReading: Three qubits carry time, type, and a passive state label.
One extra qubit makes enough room for a reversible completion.
When the signal starts and ends at 0, the system block equals E1.
The remaining basis states are filled in only to make the full map bijective/unitary.

theorems.label: Case theorem
theorems.title: The clean ancilla block equals the finite transfer operator
theorems.statementProse: The constructed full basis map is a permutation, hence unitary, and every clean-block matrix entry agrees with E1 exactly with alpha=1.
proofSteps: Specify the desired partial action
Only the labelled input sector (t,y)=(1,1) should move to (0,0); the passive state bit is unchanged.
Complete it reversibly
Use the signal qubit to route collisions into the complementary branch so the full basis map is bijective.
Lift the bijection to a unitary
A finite permutation of basis states gives a permutation matrix.
Project the clean block
Fix signal input/output to 0 and check the remaining 8 by 8 block equals E1.

improvement.title: The same exact operator with a shallower reversible circuit
improvement.statementProse: Under one frozen logical gate convention and the lexicographic score (gate count, depth, auxiliary qubits, oracle calls), Lean proves two strict improvements while the clean block stays unchanged.
proofSteps: First reduction
Remove redundant gates from the direct completion and re-prove the same permutation and clean block.
Parallelize
Rewrite the final candidate so three X operations occupy one parallel layer after a Toffoli.
Recompute resources
The score is derived from the declared circuit/schedule rather than typed by hand.
Compare in Lean
The betterThan theorems prove strict lexicographic dominance only after correctness has already passed.

be-case-1-isolated-baseline.readerGoal: Separate reproducible proof construction from claims about an agent rediscovering an answer.
be-case-1-isolated-baseline.whyThisCase: A benchmark can accidentally become easy if the solver retrieves its previous answer. This case freezes the same E1 contract but reconstructs a different exact reversible completion in an isolated route.
be-case-1-isolated-baseline.algorithmContext: The mathematics is the same block-encoding problem as BE Case 1. The scientific question is different: does an independent construction still reach a valid certificate?
circuitReading: The target, ancilla convention, and alpha=1 are fixed before construction.
A five-gate reversible circuit implements a different full-space completion.
Lean checks bijectivity and the same clean 8 by 8 block.
There is one scored candidate, so the page does not call it a resource winner or a fresh model discovery.

theorems.label: Case theorem
theorems.title: An isolated permutation also block-encodes E1
theorems.statementProse: The isolated basis map is bijective, its clean block is E1, and its resource record is exact for the declared logical circuit.
proofSteps: Build the image table
Define where every finite basis state goes.
Prove it is a bijection
No two inputs collide and every output is reached.
Check the clean rows and columns
The signal-zero submatrix is exactly E1.
Package the cost
The score is attached to this route without comparing it to a different semantic tier.

cubic-diagonal-cold.readerGoal: See how a whole symbolic family of non-unitary diagonal matrices can receive an exact block-encoding proof.
cubic-diagonal-cold.whyThisCase: Scientific algorithms often need functions of an index, coordinate, or eigenvalue. The target here multiplies basis state |j> by the cubic value (j/2^n)^3, which is generally not unitary and therefore cannot simply be declared a gate.
cubic-diagonal-cold.algorithmContext: Diagonal function loaders are natural ingredients for matrix functions, coefficient operators, Hamiltonians, and QSVT-style pipelines. This case focuses on the block-encoding construction itself.
circuitReading: The n system qubits hold j and are not overwritten.
Three clean qubits provide coordinates for an exact rational unit vector.
For each j, a Householder transformation has the desired cubic value as its clean matrix entry.
Selecting the first branch coordinate returns the diagonal entry (j/2^n)^3.

theorems.label: Family theorem
theorems.title: Exact rational Householder block encoding for every n
theorems.statementProse: For arbitrary n, Lean constructs exact rational branch vectors, proves their normalization, proves the controlled Householder operator is orthogonal/unitary, and proves every clean diagonal entry equals the cubic target with alpha=1.
proofSteps: Fix one desired diagonal value
For each j, let c=(j/2^n)^3, which lies in [0,1].
Complete c to an exact rational unit vector
Use a four-square witness to express 1-c^2 as a sum of rational squares.
Build a Householder reflection
A reflection constructed from that vector is rational and orthogonal.
Control by j
Take the direct sum of the appropriate reflection for every computational-basis label j.
Project the clean coordinate
The first branch coordinate of the direct sum is exactly diag(c_j).

cubic-diagonal-hinted.readerGoal: Learn the difference between a useful mathematical hint and a proof of the resulting quantum circuit.
cubic-diagonal-hinted.whyThisCase: A human hint says to first encode x_j=j/2^n and then think of the cubic target as x_j^3. That idea is valuable for choosing a route, but it does not by itself establish unitarity or a clean block.
cubic-diagonal-hinted.algorithmContext: This mirrors how research actually proceeds: algebra suggests a decomposition, while each quantum-access object still needs its own exact certificate.
circuitReading: Construct an exact block encoding of O0=diag(x_j).
The current library separately certifies an exact cubic Householder block rather than pretending the prose hint is a primitive QSVT circuit.
No strict resource comparison is claimed because the two constructions use different branch widths and no betterThan theorem connects them.

theorems.label: Route theorem
theorems.title: The linear input and cubic output blocks are both exact
theorems.statementProse: Lean certifies the linear diagonal block and the cubic diagonal block as separate exact constructions; the identity D_n=O0^3 explains the hint but does not replace those certificates.
proofSteps: Formalize the hint
Turn the prose suggestion into the two precise operator targets O0 and Dn.
Certify O0
Construct a rational Householder clean block with first coordinate x_j.
Identify the desired polynomial
The target diagonal entry is exactly x_j^3.
Certify Dn
Use the independent exact cubic Householder family theorem.
Keep QSVT honest
Do not label a polynomial identity as a synthesized QSVT phase sequence unless that separate route is proved.

robin-ghl-one-term.readerGoal: Follow a research paper from the access model assumed by quantum algorithms all the way to a gate-level block encoding, then compare it with an evolved exact circuit.
robin-ghl-one-term.whyThisCase: Hamiltonian-simulation papers often begin by saying 'assume an oracle for H' or 'assume a block encoding of H'. Guseynov, Huang, and Liu ask what it actually costs to build that access for finite-difference PDE operators with Robin boundaries and piecewise coefficients. Their goal is explicit gate-level construction rather than leaving matrix access as a black box.
robin-ghl-one-term.algorithmContext: The full pipeline is: discretize the PDE -> homogenize and Schrodingerise it -> obtain a Hermitian Hamiltonian H -> construct a block encoding U_H -> feed U_H to QSVT/Hamiltonian simulation to approximate exp(-iHt) -> postselect auxiliary registers to recover the solution state. The paper assumes the initial PDE condition is already provided as a quantum state, and explicitly warns that state-preparation and measurement costs can erase an apparent speedup.

source.title: Quantum Framework for Simulating Linear PDEs with Robin Boundary Conditions
source.authors: Nikita Guseynov, Xiajie Huang, Nana Liu
source.shortQuote: how to account for the cost of representing problem structure
source.queryExplanation: A digital query oracle returns the binary representation of one Hamiltonian entry. Counting one oracle call as one abstract operation can hide the arithmetic, boundary logic, and ancilla needed to implement it. GHL instead constructs amplitude/block-encoding circuits explicitly and counts CNOTs and one-qubit rotations.

pipeline: Start with a linear PDE containing derivatives, variable coefficients, a source term, and Robin boundary conditions.
Replace spatial derivatives by a sparse matrix A on N=2^n grid points. Boundary rows differ from the periodic bulk.
Embed the non-Hermitian evolution into a larger Hermitian Hamiltonian H so it can be simulated by unitary quantum dynamics.
Build an explicit unitary U_H whose clean ancilla block equals H/alpha.
Use the block encoding as the input oracle for a polynomial transformation approximating exp(-iHt).
Apply the evolution to the encoded initial state and postselect the auxiliary registers to recover a state proportional to the PDE solution.
circuitReading: The sparse selector s says which finite-difference band/position is being addressed; the system register j stores the grid index.
Create a coherent superposition over sparse slots instead of classically looping over them.
Mark whether j belongs to the periodic-like bulk or the Robin boundary region.
Turn a normalized matrix coefficient into an amplitude on a clean coefficient qubit.
Reversibly move from (slot,column) to the matrix row addressed by that slot.
Undo temporary address/indicator information so the selected ancillas return to |0>; only then does the clean projected block have the desired matrix meaning.

theorems.label: GHL Theorem 3 · source theorem, faithfully restated
theorems.title: One-term block encoding for f(x) times a sparse Robin derivative
theorems.statementFormula: A_k\sim f(x)\,\frac{\partial^m}{\partial x^m},\qquad U_{A_k}^{(1)}\text{ is an }(N_DN_f\kappa,\lceil\log_2n\rceil+\lceil\log_2G_f\rceil+\lceil\log_2\kappa\rceil+4,0)\text{-block encoding}
theorems.statementProse: For a piecewise-continuous coefficient f with G_f pieces and polynomial complexity Q_g, and a 2^n by 2^n kappa-sparse finite-difference derivative matrix with Robin boundaries, the paper constructs a one-term block encoding. Its stated gate complexity is O(sum_g Q_g n log n + kappa n) with 2n pure ancillas.
proofSteps: Exploit periodic bulk
Away from the boundary, the Robin stencil agrees with the familiar periodic stencil, so one reusable sparse-amplitude construction handles most indices.
Mark the boundary
An indicator qubit distinguishes bulk indices from the O(1)-width boundary region.
Load derivative coefficients
Use the sparse derivative amplitude oracle in the bulk and controlled RY rotations for individual boundary entries.
Apply sparse access
A reversible banded-sparse-access map transports the selector and grid index to the matrix location required by the derivative stencil.
Load f(x)
Multiply in the piecewise coefficient through its amplitude/block-encoding construction.
Swap and uncompute
Transport the registers back through the inverse access maps so workspace is clean.
Read the clean block
PREPARE/unprepare interference leaves A_k/(N_D N_f kappa) in the ancilla-zero block.
theorems.formalizationScope: Paper scope: an arbitrary-width one-term construction with the stated asymptotic resource bound. Lean scope: the theorem metadata and reusable sparse-access semantics are formalized, and the N=8 Figure-4 specialization is closed through an exact primitive VerifiedOperatorBlockEncoding. A uniform arbitrary-width primitive compiler proving every source-oracle gate bound remains a separate planned frontier; the fixed-N=8 roots below must not be read as that stronger compiler theorem.

theorems.label: GHL Theorem 4 · source theorem, faithfully restated
theorems.title: Combine the one-term blocks into the full Schrodingerised Hamiltonian
theorems.statementProse: The paper states that the structured one-dimensional Hamiltonian H has an O(kappa ||H||_max)-normalized block encoding using logarithmic selector/register overhead, with total gate complexity obtained from the coefficient-function loaders, the one-term sparse derivative blocks, and the x_xi diagonal block. The theorem reports 2n+2 pure ancillas.
proofSteps: Build every A_k
Use the one-term result for each coefficient-times-derivative term.
LCU to form A
Combine the A_k block encodings into a block encoding of A=sum_k A_k; the adjoint circuit gives A^dagger.
Build B and x_xi
Use the diagonal-function block-encoding theorem for the source/homogenization block B and the Schrodingerisation coordinate x_xi.
LCU to form S1 and S2
Combine controlled A/A^dagger with X tensor B and Y tensor B so the clean blocks become the two Hermitian matrices S1 and S2.
Final LCU
Combine U_S1, U_S2, and the block encoding of x_xi one last time to obtain H.
Source-fidelity audit

ASPBE also checks the printed phase choices in the first S1 LCU line: the literal full-clean-matrix reading leaves a filler term, so the site records the discrepancy and the phase-balanced correction instead of silently changing the paper.
theorems.formalizationScope: Paper scope: the one-dimensional A-to-H Hamiltonian composition. Lean scope: the finite-sum adjoint bridge, S1/S2 clean-block algebra, final H formula, normalization/layout records, and the source phase audit are compiled. The printed first S1 phase pair is proved inconsistent under the literal full-clean-matrix reading, and a phase-balanced correction is separately proved before the aggregate Theorem-4 route is marked closed.

benchmarkBridge.title: Why the website then freezes N=8
benchmarkBridge.body: The source theorem is a symbolic family statement. To compare actual circuits gate by gate, ASPBE freezes the N=8 Eq. (9) specialization with A1=B1=0, factors out Delta x^{-2}, and fixes alpha=56/3. That gives one exact matrix on which the source Figure-4 realization, a simpler paper-seven normal form, and an evolved candidate can all be compiled to the same primitive basis and compared without changing the target.

sourceAssumptions.title: A query oracle is an access contract, not a free physical gate
sourceAssumptions.paperAssumption: The paper contrasts an abstract digital matrix-entry query O_H with explicit sparse-access and amplitude/block-encoding circuits.
sourceAssumptions.plainLanguage: When an algorithm says it makes one query, it means one call to a promised reversible data-access subroutine. The arithmetic, memory lookup, boundary tests, and ancillas hidden inside that call may still be expensive to build.
sourceAssumptions.whyItMatters: GHL's construction is useful precisely because it opens this black box for the structured Robin operator; ASPBE therefore reports oracle calls separately from primitive gates.

sourceAssumptions.title: Figure 4 applies its bulk indicator to D-transpose
sourceAssumptions.paperAssumption: The source circuit's indicator is interpreted on a row of D-transpose, so the fixed N=8 realization selects the corresponding columns of D rather than a naively read row window.
sourceAssumptions.plainLanguage: The circuit is moving between row and column viewpoints. Reading the indicator against the wrong orientation changes which boundary entries receive special treatment.
sourceAssumptions.whyItMatters: This choice changes the executable circuit, so ASPBE proves the transported bulk action before accepting the Figure-4 clean block.

sourceAssumptions.title: Standard RY uses a half angle
sourceAssumptions.paperAssumption: Equation (27) prints a single arccos coefficient angle; under the standard RY(theta) convention the executable angle must be 2 arccos(c).
sourceAssumptions.plainLanguage: An RY rotation places cos(theta/2), not cos(theta), in the clean amplitude. To load coefficient c exactly, theta must therefore equal 2 arccos(c).
sourceAssumptions.whyItMatters: Using the printed single-arccos expression would certify the wrong amplitude. ASPBE retains the typo transcript but proves the corrected standard-RY circuit.

sourceAssumptions.title: Seven source slots are an LCU decomposition, not a sparse-enumeration oracle
sourceAssumptions.paperAssumption: The historical split-seven weighted-permutation representation can send distinct nonzero slots to the same matrix entry.
sourceAssumptions.plainLanguage: Two selector labels may contribute amplitudes to the same matrix location. That is legal for a linear-combination-of-unitaries construction, but it is not the promise made by a one-nonzero-per-slot sparse enumerator.
sourceAssumptions.whyItMatters: Treating the seven labels as a sparse oracle would silently strengthen the access promise. ASPBE instead proves the weighted-permutation sum and records the duplicate access explicitly.

sourceAssumptions.title: Only the clean projected block is the encoded operator
sourceAssumptions.paperAssumption: Temporary selector, indicator, coefficient, and address workspaces are uncomputed before the clean block is read.
sourceAssumptions.plainLanguage: A block encoding does not claim that the full unitary equals the PDE matrix. It claims that when designated ancillas start and end at zero, the selected submatrix equals the normalized target.
sourceAssumptions.whyItMatters: Full-space behavior on dirty workspace states may be compiler-dependent; the theorem must therefore prove the declared zero-workspace projection, not an informal whole-unitary equality.

sourceAssumptions.title: The Theorem-4 phase discrepancy is recorded, not silently repaired
sourceAssumptions.paperAssumption: With Eq. (29)'s filler convention, the printed first-line phases pi and -pi in Eq. (30) both contribute -1 and leave a nonzero lower-right filler block.
sourceAssumptions.plainLanguage: The two printed phases do not cancel: exp(i*pi)=exp(-i*pi)=-1. A literal matrix sum therefore cannot equal the displayed S1 block unless the filler is corrected.
sourceAssumptions.whyItMatters: Source fidelity requires distinguishing what the paper prints from the corrected executable identity. Lean proves the obstruction and then proves a phase-balanced S1 construction; S2 closes as printed.

sourceAssumptions.title: The 106-vs-312-vs-881 claim lives on one frozen compiler tier
sourceAssumptions.paperAssumption: For the N=8 comparison, all candidates use exact {X, RY, RZ, CX} primitive programs, all-to-all connectivity, the same target/normalizer, and zero abstract oracle calls.
sourceAssumptions.plainLanguage: Resource numbers are comparable only after the target, gate vocabulary, connectivity, ancilla convention, and oracle accounting have been frozen. Otherwise a smaller number may simply be using a different cost model.
sourceAssumptions.whyItMatters: ASPBE's winner is a strict same-tier theorem, not a universal circuit lower bound. The evolved circuit is better in gate count, depth, and auxiliary-qubit coordinates while oracle calls stay equal.

improvement.title: Evolved theorem: a strictly cheaper exact block encoding for the frozen Robin benchmark
improvement.statementProse: All three circuits encode the same dimensionless N=8 target with alpha=56/3, zero error, the same exact primitive basis {X,RY,RZ,CX}, the same all-to-all connectivity convention, and clean workspaces. Lean certifies the XOR four-slot circuit and proves both strict comparisons. This is a benchmark/compiler theorem, not a global lower bound over all possible quantum circuits.
proofSteps: Use centrosymmetry
Pair matrix indices related by reversal so the 8 by 8 target decomposes into two smaller symmetry sectors.
Use four XOR slots
Within each sector, index the required positions by two selector bits using XOR rather than a carry-producing modular adder.
Load exact amplitudes
A uniformly controlled RY compiler realizes the 32 exact coefficient branches with structured exact-angle semantics.
Simplify SELECT
The XOR addressing rule reduces SELECT to two CX gates on the pair-coordinate bits.
Refine to primitives
Lean proves the product of the emitted X/RY/RZ/CX gates equals the previously verified logical unitary, not merely a floating-point approximation.
Inherit the clean-block theorem
Exact primitive equality transports the already-proved logical clean block to the primitive circuit.
Compute and compare cost
Resource tuples are derived from the primitive programs and the betterThan theorems establish strict same-tier dominance.
